mcqs.question: A team puts a freshly-fetched list of posts into the same global store as the app's modal-open/closed flags and active-tab selection. What's the problem with this?
options: Global stores cannot hold arrays, only primitives
It conflates client-cache state (server-originated, can go stale) with UI state (ephemeral, local), making it unclear which parts need revalidation and which don't
Modal open/closed flags must always be stored in the URL, never in a store
It will cause a memory leak because arrays are never garbage collected
mcqs.explanation: Client cache mirrors server data and can go stale, needing its own invalidation logic; UI state is ephemeral and local. Mixing them in one bucket makes it unclear which entries need revalidation, which is the exact confusion this topic's three-layer model resolves. Arrays are a normal store value, and there's no inherent memory-leak or URL requirement here.

mcqs.question: A feed screen and a comments screen each independently embed a full copy of the same author object in their cached data. A user updates their display name. What does normalization fix here?
options: Normalization removes the need to ever refetch data from the server
Normalization automatically renames the user across the backend database
Normalization stores the author once in a shared users-by-ID table, so both screens reference the same entity and update together instead of holding two independent stale copies
Normalization converts the REST API into a GraphQL API
mcqs.explanation: Normalizing means keeping one canonical copy per entity keyed by ID, with every reference elsewhere pointing to that ID — so updating the shared users table reflects everywhere instantly. It doesn't touch the backend database, doesn't eliminate refetching, and has nothing to do with the API protocol.

mcqs.question: An app has many screens showing overlapping views of the same entities, and manually tracking which mutation should invalidate which cached query has become error-prone. Which invalidation strategy is built for exactly this?
options: Time-based invalidation, since a short enough TTL makes tagging unnecessary
Event-based invalidation triggered only by the client's own mutations
Never invalidating, and instead relying on a full page reload
Tag-based invalidation, where each query is tagged with the entities it reads and any mutation invalidates every entry sharing that tag
mcqs.explanation: Tag-based invalidation is designed for exactly this many-to-many overlap — tagging queries by the entities they touch means one mutation can correctly invalidate every affected view without hand-tracking each pairing. A short TTL only bounds staleness, it doesn't solve the tracking problem, event-based alone misses cross-screen effects, and reloading the page defeats the purpose of caching at all.

mcqs.question: In the optimistic-update code sample, why does `onMutate` return `{ previous }` instead of just updating the cache and returning nothing?
options: Returning a value is required by JavaScript syntax for any function passed to `useMutation`
`{ previous }` becomes the context passed to `onError`, which is the only way to restore the exact prior cache value if the mutation fails
It has no functional purpose and is only used for TypeScript type inference
It tells React Query to skip calling `onSettled` afterward
mcqs.explanation: The snapshot captured before the optimistic write is passed forward as mutation context, and `onError` uses it to restore precisely what was there — without it, a failed mutation has no reliable prior value to roll back to. It isn't a syntax requirement, isn't purely cosmetic, and doesn't affect whether `onSettled` runs.

mcqs.question: Which action is the weakest candidate for an optimistic update?
options: Liking a post
Deleting a draft comment (reversible via undo)
Toggling a UI theme preference
Confirming a payment charge, where success isn't guaranteed and a false 'success' briefly shown erodes trust
mcqs.explanation: Optimistic updates trade a small chance of a visible correction for perceived speed — a bet that only pays off when failure is cheap and honest to show. A payment charge is exactly the case where showing 'success' before it's real is worse than a brief wait, unlike likes, reversible deletes, or purely local preferences.

mcqs.question: A feed item copies `post.likeCount` into its own local component state on mount so it can update it locally, while a detail modal reads the same post from the shared cache. What bug does this cause?
options: The feed item and the modal can show different like counts for the same post after one of them changes, because there are now two unsynchronized copies of the same entity
The app will throw a runtime error because two components cannot read the same post
The modal will always show a newer value than the feed item
This pattern has no downside as long as both components eventually re-fetch
mcqs.explanation: Copying a server entity into local state forks a second copy that the shared cache's updates never reach, so the two components can silently disagree — exactly the bug the single-source-of-truth rule prevents. There's no runtime error, no guaranteed direction to the drift, and 'eventually re-fetch' isn't guaranteed to happen at all without explicit wiring.
